title: Deprecation
checklist: Annotate the member @deprecated since TYPO3 v<the version this lands in>, will be removed in TYPO3 v<the next major>. and close that line with the migration sentence. Read both versions off the branch you are on rather than off an example.

Keep the member working and open its body with trigger_error('<Class>-><member>() is deprecated since TYPO3 v<the version this lands in> and will be removed in TYPO3 v<the next major>. <migration>', E_USER_DEPRECATED). The docblock and the message say the same three things, and the removal is a patch of its own in that major.
Migrate every caller of the deprecated API in the same patch, and confirm none is left behind.

Add a changelog file below typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/<the minor this is released in>/ named Deprecation-<issue>-<UpperCamelCaseDescription>.rst. Nothing has to include it: that directory's Index.rst pulls Deprecation-* in by glob, so the filename is the inclusion.

Open the changelog file with .. include:: /Includes.rst.txt and a unique .. _deprecation-<issue>-<unix timestamp>: anchor directly above the 'Deprecation: #<issue> - <title>' headline, with See :issue:`<issue>` under it. Then Description, Impact, Affected installations and Migration — the last two are what this type owes over a feature entry.

End the changelog file with .. index:: carrying at least one subject tag and exactly one of FullyScanned, PartiallyScanned or NotScanned. Build/Scripts/validateRstFiles.php rejects a Deprecation file without the scanner tag, so it is owed rather than considered.

Back a FullyScanned or PartiallyScanned tag with an extension scanner matcher: an entry below typo3/sysext/install/Configuration/ExtensionScanner/Php/, keyed by the deprecated symbol and naming the changelog file in its restFiles. NotScanned is for what no matcher can find, not for what nobody wrote.
Use [TASK] or [FEATURE] as the commit keyword. A deprecation must never use the [!!!] breaking prefix.
tools: typo3_commit_message_guide with workflow="core" and isDeprecation=true, to get the keyword and prefix rules checked

title: Breaking change
checklist: Settle first that the change is breaking at all: @internal says the API is not public and does not decide it, and what does is whether anything outside the core calls it. The core has removed @internal members both ways. A change that moves no member is settled on what it renders instead, which typo3_hint_lookup with the id breaking-without-a-moved-member states.
Add a changelog file below typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/<version>/ named Breaking-<issue>-<Title>.rst.
Prefix the commit summary with [!!!] before the keyword.
Target main; confirm any older release target with the release managers.
Describe the migration path for extension authors.

Add an extension scanner matcher entry below typo3/sysext/install/Configuration/ExtensionScanner/Php/ for every method, property and class the changelog entry removes, with restFiles naming that entry. Which file takes which kind of removal is in the Breaking Changes section typo3_rule_lookup answers with.
Tag the changelog entry NotScanned, PartiallyScanned or FullyScanned for what those matchers actually reach.
tools: typo3_commit_message_guide with workflow="core" and isBreaking=true

title: Changelog or ReST documentation
checklist: Changelog files live below typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/, in the directory of the minor version the change is released in; a backport goes into the <lts>.x directory of the oldest branch it reaches. The file is named <Type>-<forgeIssueNumber>-<UpperCamelCaseDescription>.rst.

The type is the first of four that describes the change: Breaking where it moves or removes core functionality third-party code may use, Deprecation where it marks core functionality for a planned removal, Feature where it adds functionality, Important for anything else that may require manual action and the only one an LTS release may carry. A casual bug fix owes no entry. There is no Task type; checkRst fails a title opening with anything else.

Fill in the skeleton the type owes rather than copying a neighbour: the include, the anchor, the fenced title, the See :issue: line, the sections that type carries, and the .. index:: tags the file ends on.
tools: typo3_hint_lookup with id=documentation-changelog, for that skeleton and the tags the file ends on

title: User-facing labels
condition: only if the change adds, edits, or retires an XLF trans-unit
checklist: Reference labels by their translation domain (package.resource:key), not by the EXT: file path. typo3_translation_domain_lookup computes the domain of any XLF path.
Never delete a trans-unit: mark it x-unused-since="<next version>" and remove it in a later major.
Write the source unit in English. A translation maintained in the package belongs in the locale-prefixed XLF beside that source file.

Correct a source file that is not English in place: same path, same unit ids, English wording, and the wording it replaced moved into the locale-prefixed file beside it as <target> under source-language="en" target-language="<locale>". Adding an en.-prefixed file is not the correction — the unprefixed file is the default locale every other locale falls back to.
tools: typo3_translation_domain_lookup, for the domain an XLF file resolves to

title: Adding or changing a backend module
checklist: Settle where the module sits before it is named: which module it hangs under, where it stands among that parent's children, and who may open it. The identifier is what the route, the module's persisted per-user state and a user's bookmarks are keyed by, so a later rename is an alias kept beside the module rather than an edit to it.

Read the modules this installation already registers before choosing that place. A parent that is not there and an identifier that is taken are written the same way as a working one, and both fail when a user opens the module rather than when the file is saved.

Answer who may open the module and what a request inside it may read as two questions. The access declared on the registration decides the first — the entry in the tree, and the route behind it — and says nothing about the second, so a module showing records somebody else owns checks that itself.

Prove the module by opening it: the entry appears where it was placed, the route answers, the icon renders instead of an empty box, the labels resolve instead of showing their keys, and the access declared lets in whom it claims to. None of the five fails at build time, and a green test suite reports none of them.
tools: typo3_backend_module_lookup, before choosing the identifier, the parent or the route: it reports what this installation already registers
typo3_hint_lookup with id=backend-modules, for the registration file, what a module builds into its doc header, and what its own POST answers with
typo3_translation_domain_lookup, for the XLF the module's labels are declared through

title: Backend UI markup
condition: only if the change adds or alters backend component markup or CSS classes
checklist: Use the existing backend component classes and their documented markup instead of new ad-hoc classes.
Check the styleguide demo of the component for the canonical structure.
tools: typo3_component_lookup, before writing backend markup or CSS classes

title: Icons
checklist: Resolve the icon identifier in your own checkout before using it: IconRegistry is built from every installed package, so an identifier that exists in one instance may not exist in another, and an unknown one only fails at runtime.

title: Test coverage
checklist: Confirm the test fails without the change and passes with it.
Run the single test file or method while iterating instead of the whole suite.
tools: typo3_test_run_guide, for the targeted invocation form
typo3_hint_lookup id=project-extension-tests, where the extension is not part of the core and the suite has to be assembled first

title: Browser tests
checklist: Read skills/typo3-extension-testing/references/playwright.md before writing the first spec. It is the implementation guide for this layer and this brief does not repeat what it carries.
Keep the suite with what is deployed rather than with the package: a spec needs a served site and a real URL, which an extension package alone does not have.
tools: typo3_hint_lookup id=browser-tests, for the layout the core's own suite established and what a backend spec has to locate through
typo3_hint_lookup id=browser-tests-outside-core, for the site a suite outside the core runs against

title: Coding standards and the code style fixer
condition: only if the change establishes or runs a code style check rather than editing code the check happens to cover
checklist: Read what the repository already has before adding anything: a .php-cs-fixer.dist.php, an .editorconfig, a Composer script naming either, and a CI step calling one. Half an infrastructure is the ordinary case, and a second rule set beside an existing one is a second answer to maintain.

Take the rule set from typo3/coding-standards rather than assembling one, and let the solver pick the release: the package is below 1.0 and its PHP floor decides which one the extension's declared range can have.
Keep the check and the fix as two commands. The fixing run exits 0 whether it rewrote the tree or not, so only the dry run is a verdict CI can read.

Confirm what the fixer's paths actually reach with its own dry run before the first write, and read the file list rather than the summary. The shipped extension configuration scans the whole package directory, and what an installed TYPO3 beneath it costs depends on where that installation was put.

Where the tree does not pass the check yet, the conformance commits come first and the commit adding the check comes last, so no commit fails the check it introduces. Verify by running the check at the new HEAD.
tools: typo3_hint_lookup with id=extension-coding-standards, for what typo3/coding-standards ships, what its setup command writes, what the configuration already excludes and which run is the check
typo3_hint_lookup with id=extension-static-analysis, for the analyser half of the same layer
typo3_project_describe, for the TYPO3 and PHP range the package declares and the commands it already has

title: Patch submission
condition: if the patch goes to the TYPO3 core itself
checklist: One patch is one commit: improve it by amending, never by adding a second commit.
Push with git push origin HEAD:refs/for/<branch> and keep the Change-Id line untouched.
tools: typo3_commit_message_guide with workflow="core", to check the message before pushing

title: Fetching a change from review
condition: if the patch is one somebody pushed to review.typo3.org
checklist: Fetch the patch set the change is on rather than the one a link happens to name. A change is a series of patch sets, and reading an older one is a review of code nobody is proposing.

A patch that no longer applies is a finding: the branch moved under a change nobody rebased. Resolving your way to something that compiles destroys that finding and produces a patch its author never wrote, so a conflict you cannot take from the change itself ends the work with what it found.

Leave the checkout on a clean current branch when you are done or when the patch will not apply. A fetched change sitting on a detached head is the state the next session cannot tell from its own work, and a branch you carried the patch onto is that state under a name: delete it as deliberately as you made it.
tools: typo3_gerrit_lookup with change=<number>, for the patch set the change is actually on and the commit to hold the checkout against

title: Issue triage
condition: if the report is one on forge.typo3.org
checklist: A report is about the version it was filed against and never about the one in front of you. Establish what it still claims in the checkout you are standing in, and say which branch that was.

Read the comments before the description. The description is what the reporter saw; whether the report was accepted, reverted or reclassified is in the journal, and on a long-lived issue the note that settles it is regularly the last of them.
A relation marked precedes or duplicates is usually where a previous attempt was filed. What that attempt cost is what answers "what would this cost", and it is one read rather than a guess.

A verdict names what would change it: the branch it was established on, the file it was established in, and what a maintainer would need before the issue can move. "Cannot be settled without X" is a result and ends the work honestly.
tools: typo3_forge_lookup with open="oldest" or open="stale" to find candidates, then issue=<number> to read one whole; notes="people" drops the patch-set pings when reading many
typo3_gerrit_lookup for the changes the issue answer's reviews field names, which is where an abandoned attempt says why

title: Review or audit
checklist: Where the review is of a change, enumerate what it removes or renames before judging it: the public classes, methods and properties it takes away, and the signature of anything that stays. A task text names what a change is about and never what it takes away, so this is the one surface no other item here can state for you.

Hold each removal in a core patch to what it owes, in the diff rather than in the summary: a matcher entry below typo3/sysext/install/Configuration/ExtensionScanner/Php/ keyed by the removed symbol, a Breaking or Deprecation changelog file its restFiles names, and the [!!!] prefix where the change is breaking. @internal on the member does not settle whether it is — whether anything outside the core calls it does, and the core has removed @internal members both ways.

Run CI=true ./Build/Scripts/runTests.sh -s checkRst and CI=true ./Build/Scripts/runTests.sh -s checkExtensionScannerRst over a core diff that removes something. The second holds a matcher to the changelog file it names and nothing holds a changelog to the matcher it lacks, so a missing matcher is found by reading the removals against the matcher files.

A finding names the location, what the code there does, and the rule or documentation it contradicts. Short of those three it is a question rather than a violation, and reporting it as one costs the maintainer exactly the reading the review skipped.

Run the checks this repository declares rather than recommending them, and read a green result as what its commands cover: an entry no command covers is a gap in the check layer, which is a finding of its own.
Hand each finding over with its consequence and what would remediate it, and route the work to whoever does it. A review changes nothing itself, so the report is what it produces.
tools: typo3_project_describe, for the TYPO3 and PHP versions this repository supports and the commands it declares
typo3_extension_describe, for what each extension in scope registers

title: Putting a repository right
condition: only if the task asks for the repository as a whole to be changed rather than reviewed, or for the findings of a review to be worked off
checklist: Run the audit before writing the list, and let it own the findings: what a surface is, what evidence a finding rests on, what it is worth and who fixes it are the conformance workflow's answers. A list built from a reading of the checkout instead is an impression, and the items in it are not the ones the report would have given.

Show the list whole and let the maintainer cut items, reorder them or stop, before a single file is changed. That agreement is the one step nothing downstream recovers, and a list arriving with the changes it produced is one nobody had the chance to disagree with.

Keep the list in the reply rather than committing it into the repository. A worklist committed into somebody's history is a file nobody asked for that has to be taken out again; what the history keeps is the commits the items produced, each saying which item it closed.

Work an item in the workflow that owns it, and stop before editing files another owner has. An item no workflow owns is worked here only where the project's own suite, linter or static analysis proves the change — anything else goes back unassigned, because a finding nobody owns and no check covers is a hole in the workflow map and quietly filling it hides the hole.

Hand the worked list back for the re-check rather than grading it. A cleanup that declares its own findings gone has no evidence for it, and the audit kept that responsibility when it handed each finding over.
Report the items still open, the ones dropped with what dropped them, and the ones sent back unassigned. A finished list and an abandoned one read alike in a summary.
tools: typo3_project_describe, for what the repository is before anything in it is changed
typo3_extension_describe, for what each extension in scope registers
typo3_commit_message_guide with workflow="project", for the message each item's commit carries

title: Setting an installation up
condition: only if the task is setting an installation up rather than working on the code in one
checklist: State the admin username and the password in your reply, with the URL of the backend they belong to. The setup command prints neither, so where it ran non-interactively the party that chose the value is the only one that has it — and a password nobody reports is a lockout of the installation that was just created.

Generate that password rather than inventing a quiet default, and keep it out of the shell history: --admin-user-password and TYPO3_SETUP_ADMIN_PASSWORD both end up in it, which is what the command's own help warns about. The interactive mode avoids it, and so does a leading space in bash and zsh.

The same value becomes the install tool password. The command creates the backend user and then sets BE/installToolPassword in config/system/settings.php to what it was handed, and there is no option of its own for it — so the two start out identical and diverge silently the first time somebody changes the backend password.

Neither is stored reversibly, so recovery is a reset and not a lookup: backend:resetpassword for the backend user, and for the install tool the BE/installToolPassword hash in config/system/settings.php — which install:password:set rewrites where the installation has that command.

Leave --create-site out where a sitepackage ships a root page and a site configuration. It creates both itself, and the sitepackage's own import then lands beside them: a second root page, and its site configuration skipped because the identifier already exists.

Settle what the command takes before writing the command line: typo3_hint_lookup with id=installation-setup says which connection types --driver accepts against the driver name that lands in config/system/settings.php, that sqlite needs no credentials at all, that a database with tables in it is refused, and that --create-site and --distribution do nothing in Composer mode wherever a required package ships an Initialisation/ data file — which is where an installation ends up with no site configuration and no way to be told its own URL.
tools: typo3_project_describe, for what the installation around this repository already is
typo3_hint_lookup with id=installation-setup, for what typo3 setup accepts, what it refuses, and which of its options are inert in Composer mode
typo3_hint_lookup with id=sitepackage-initial-content, for what a sitepackage seeds an empty installation with and why the order of the two setup commands decides it

title: Upgrading or maintaining an installation
condition: only if the task is about an installation rather than about the code in it
checklist: Establish where you are before changing anything: typo3_project_describe for the installed TYPO3 and PHP and for which extensions are the project's own, typo3_changelog_lookup with type=breaking for what the target version did to them.
Check every third-party extension for a release that supports the target major. One that has none decides the schedule, and Composer reports it as a conflict rather than as advice.
Dump the database and work on a copy. From the first schema change on, the upgrade cannot be reverted with git.
Raise the PHP version where the target requires it — in composer.json and in the environment that runs it — then require the new TYPO3 constraints together with every extension in one composer call.
Then, in this order: typo3 extension:setup for the schema and the static data, typo3 upgrade:list and typo3 upgrade:run for the wizards, typo3 cache:flush.

Run the Extension Scanner over the project's own extensions for the call sites the changelog named, and re-check the site configuration, the TypoScript and the TSconfig — then repeat the same commands in the same order on every other environment.
tools: typo3_project_describe, for what this installation is and which commands this repository declares
typo3_changelog_lookup with type=breaking or deprecation and the target version
typo3_hint_lookup with id=installation-upgrade, for the order of operations and why it is that order

title: Bringing an installation up and running it
condition: only if the task is bringing an installation up or running one rather than changing the code in it
checklist: In a DDEV project the lifecycle hooks in .ddev/config.yaml — post-start, post-import-db, pre-pull, post-pull — and the pull providers under .ddev/providers/ are the install and the import: they are what installs the dependencies, updates the schema and creates the backend user, so equivalent commands typed beside them boot something this repository does not describe. typo3_project_describe reports the environment and the composer scripts, and those hooks are read from the file itself.

Where no installation exists yet, the order is typo3 setup for config/system/settings.php, the admin user and the schema, then typo3 extension:setup for the extension setup and the content a required distribution package imports, then typo3 cache:flush. The setup command refuses a database that already holds tables, so a script that runs a second time needs its own guard on settings.php — --force rewrites the settings files and not the schema.

Seed a distribution by requiring its package and running typo3 extension:setup. Since v14 the setup command's --distribution and --create-site are inert in Composer mode as soon as a required package ships Initialisation/data.xml: every Composer-required package counts as an active distribution, so the command reports that the options have no effect and writes no site configuration at all.

Since v14 a site configuration that arrives with an import lands on base /<identifier>/, because Import::processSiteConfigurations() overwrites what the export carried — the importer cannot know the URL of the installation it is importing into. A seeded installation therefore answers 404 at its own root until that base is corrected in config/sites/<identifier>/config.yaml, and the cause is not in the distribution package.

A second site under the same host is the other way a frontend answers 404 while the backend works. TYPO3 matches every site's routes at once and a base carrying a host beats a bare path, so the site on base: / loses every request to the one that names the host, whatever the two paths are. Give the second site that host in its base as well, and read every site's base with typo3_project_describe before treating the message as a slug problem.

Leave config/system/additional.php to DDEV where DDEV writes it. While the #ddev-generated marker line is in that file it is rewritten by every start that finds an installed TYPO3, and it supplies the database connection, the container's ImageMagick paths, Mailpit and SYS/trustedHostsPattern — so hand-writing those is redundant, and switching settings management off costs the trusted hosts exception the router's host name raises. Where the installation does not use DDEV's database container, on SQLite or with omit_containers: [db], that generated mysqli connection overrides what typo3 setup wrote into settings.php: take the file over by removing the marker line and leaving its database section out.

A clone is where that detection finds nothing: DDEV reads vendor/typo3/cms-core/Classes/Information/Typo3Version.php to decide the file belongs there at all, so the ddev start that necessarily precedes composer install writes no additional.php, and every request answers exception 1396795884 for the trusted hosts pattern while typo3 setup reports success. Start the environment again once the dependencies are installed — a post-start hook that installs them does not close it, because the detection runs before the hooks — or commit a project-owned additional.php that is there from the first request.

Verify by requesting the site and the backend rather than by reading a green start. DDEV's fail_on_hook_fail defaults to false, so a post-start hook that installs the instance can fail while ddev start reports success — an install hook belongs behind fail_on_hook_fail: true.

Before the boot is reported done, establish how this package expects a fresh instance to be filled and name it to the user: the shipped Initialisation/ data file, a console command it ships, a site set an existing site has to depend on, or none of them — in which case the procedure is written down only in the package's own manual, and typo3_extension_describe reports where that manual is. An installation that answers and holds nothing to look at is not yet what was asked for, and for many extensions the step is a backend module rather than anything the console can do.
tools: typo3_project_describe, for what this repository declares: the TYPO3 and PHP it runs, the environment it ships, and the commands in its composer.json

typo3_hint_lookup with id=installation-boot, for what a clone owes the installation before it answers: the schema an imported database is behind on, the caches it brought with it, the backend user nobody has the password for, the host the site configuration names, and where the files were expected
typo3_hint_lookup with id=project-configuration-files, for which file configures what in an installation, and with id=extension-asset-build for the build a repository declares
typo3_hint_lookup with id=fresh-instance-seeding, for the ways a package declares that it fills a fresh instance and for what holds when it declares none
typo3_hint_lookup with id=site-base-collision, for which of two sites answers a request when both bases fit it, and for what the 404 that shows it does and does not say
typo3_extension_describe, for what the extension being booted ships: the Initialisation/ data files, the console.command tag, the site sets and where its manual is

title: Adding or changing a content element
condition: only if the task adds or changes a content element rather than the page around it; an Extbase plugin is one of them and not the other category
checklist: Describe the editor workflow before naming a single field: who creates each piece of this element, in which order, and what translating, hiding and deleting the element does to it. The data model is the answer to that, not a choice made afterwards.

Settle whether this element needs Extbase before its rendering is designed. It is not the choice between a content element and a plugin: since v14 registerPlugin() puts a plugin into the same CType selector as any other element, and configurePlugin() renders it as lib.contentElement with an EXTBASEPLUGIN at 20. What the fork asks is whether a controller has to answer the request — reading records into a template needs no model, no repository and no controller, and pagination, a search with arguments, validation and forms are what Extbase is for. Both sides of it are their own hint: typo3_hint_lookup with id=extbase, and with id=frontend-records.

Read the answer to that off the extension rather than deciding it alone: typo3_extension_describe reports each content element with a kind of element or plugin, and a kind of plugin is the architecture this extension already has — models, repositories, controllers. Building the next element on TCA and a data processor departs from that convention, which is a decision to state rather than one to make by not noticing.

Own repeatable content in a child table of its own with type=inline. Referencing existing records is right where reuse was asked for and nesting arbitrary tt_content where nesting was; neither is a way to store a list of slides, and both are technically possible, which is why an element that skipped the workflow question ends up with one of them.
Register this element in a file of its own under Configuration/TCA/Overrides/ and give it its own TypoScript file and template, so the generic files stay what is genuinely shared.
Load the CSS and JavaScript only this element needs through the Fluid AssetCollector in its template, rather than on every page of the site.

Cover the persistence of the child records and the order they render in with functional tests. A unit test of mocks asserts the mock, and browser behaviour that was not tested is reported as untested.
tools: typo3_hint_lookup with id=content-elements, for what the element owns and how the record type is registered, then with id=extbase and id=frontend-records for the two sides of the Extbase fork
typo3_extension_describe, for the architecture this extension already has: each content element it registers with a kind of element or plugin, and the templates they render through
